title: Renewable energy

definition.text: Energy made from renewable natural resources that are replenished on a human timescale.

facts.text: The most widely used types are solar, wind, bioenergy and hydropower; the IEA defines it as energy from natural processes replenished faster than they are consumed.
Replacing fossil fuels with low-emission sources is central to net zero; renewables are also more evenly spread worldwide than fossil fuels and cut air pollution.
Solar and wind are intermittent, with lower capacity factors, while fossil, nuclear and hydropower plants can match the grid's demand; storage returns energy when production falls below consumption.
The technical potential of utility-scale solar PV, concentrated solar, onshore and offshore wind each exceeds 100 PWh per year, against global energy use of about 65 PWh in 2019.
IRENA states about 86% (187 GW) of renewable capacity added in 2022 cost less than fossil-fuel electricity; its finance report shows US$499 billion invested in 2022.
Investment in renewables, especially solar, tends to create more jobs than coal, gas or oil.
Whether nuclear power counts as renewable is debated; legal definitions usually exclude it, with Utah an exception.
Critics note renewables need more metals and minerals whose extraction can cause environmental conflict, and installations increasingly threaten conservation areas.

contested_note: Whether nuclear power counts as renewable energy is an ongoing debate.

definition.text: An abstract description of a concrete system using mathematical concepts and language.

facts.text: A model describes a system by variables and equations relating them, and is used to predict behaviour or solve specific problems.
Models can be linear or nonlinear, static or dynamic (differential or difference equations), discrete or continuous, and deterministic or stochastic.
A deductive model rests on theory, an inductive model on empirical generalization, and a 'floating' model on neither.
Strategic models used in game theory treat players as autonomous decision makers who rationally maximize an objective function.
Complexity trades simplicity against accuracy; by Occam's razor, among models of similar predictive power the simplest is preferred.

Models are checked by splitting data into training data, which set the parameters, and verification data; scope asks whether the model holds between data points (interpolation) or beyond them (extrapolation).
Models with no a priori information are black boxes and those with all necessary information are white boxes; practically all systems lie between.
